produced: 2026-09-26, by hand in the council session with the ratified prompt (docs/school-os-proposal-capability-behaviours.md §3); not by the engine; v2 after the four-seat council review of 2026-09-26 (research/level2_council.py, seats in research/level2_council/)

capabilities.name: Knowledge & academic mastery
capabilities.observable_at_16: Strong conceptual and procedural command of core subjects; can perform under examination conditions.

behaviours.statement: Counts a set of objects up to ten, touching each once and saying one number for each.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator watches the child's finger and voice keep step through the set.
behaviours.counter_example: Recites numbers to ten faster than the finger moves, skipping or double-touching objects.

behaviours.statement: Reads a familiar word aloud from a word card or a label that has no picture beside it.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator points to a word on the word wall or a label and hears it read from its letters.
behaviours.counter_example: Names the label by where it hangs and cannot read the same word on a card held elsewhere.

notes: E edit: Covering a picture is staging; word cards and labels are already on the wall. One word read is a tick in a note, not an audio file.

before.statement: Reads a familiar word aloud from a picture book with the picture covered.
before.adult_sees: The educator covers the picture and hears the word read from the letters.
before.counter_example: Says the word from memory of the story while looking at the picture.

behaviours.from_age_why: Reading a word from its letters alone, with no picture, is a Grade 1 skill; before six a child recognises words by picture and by memory of where they saw them.

behaviours.statement: Exchanges ten single blocks for one ten-rod when asked how many tens are in a pile.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the child make the exchange and name the rod as one ten.
behaviours.counter_example: Moves blocks into a row of ten without naming it as one ten.
behaviours.from_age_why: Seeing ten ones as one unit called a ten is Grade 2 place value; a younger child counts the rod as one more block, however well they count to ten.

behaviours.statement: Retells a story just heard with its beginning, middle and end in the right order.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator hears the events come in the order the story had them.
behaviours.counter_example: Names characters from the story without the events in order.

notes: E edit: Audio of one child in a circle of thirty is not realistic; a dated note naming the three events in order holds this.

behaviours.statement: Sorts a mixed set of objects by a rule the educator names, and says the rule back.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the sort match the rule and hears the child state it.
behaviours.counter_example: Sorts by a rule of their own and cannot say what it was.

behaviours.statement: Writes or forms their own name and the numerals one to nine, on paper or with tiles, from memory, so another adult reads them back.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees no model in view and a second adult reads the name and numerals back, in any script the child is learning.
behaviours.counter_example: Traces the name over a dotted model.

notes: R edit: 'Legibly on paper' makes handwriting the gate; a child with a motor disability, or one writing in another script, shows the same knowledge with tiles or in their script.
D edit: 'Legibly' is a rating word two observers will score differently; a read-back by a second adult is the agreement test.
chair edit: merged: the development seat's read-back by a second adult replaces 'legibly'; the rights seat's tiles and any script open it to every child.

before.statement: Writes their own name and the numerals one to nine legibly on paper without a model to copy.
before.adult_sees: The educator sees the writing done with no model in view.

behaviours.statement: Uses a word taught this week in a sentence of their own about something in the room.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator hears the week's word in a sentence the child made, about a thing in view.
behaviours.counter_example: Repeats the sentence the educator used to teach the word.

notes: chair add: development: oral vocabulary is the strongest foundational knowledge marker and the only one a Nursery child can show; the cell was all print and number.

behaviours.statement: Adds two three-digit numbers with regrouping on paper, showing the exchange in the working.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the carried ten written in the working, not only the total.
behaviours.counter_example: Writes the correct total with no working shown.

behaviours.statement: Reads a grade-level passage aloud and answers a question whose answer is stated in the text, reading out the line that says it.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator hears the passage read, the answer given, and the line from the text read out as its source.
behaviours.counter_example: Answers from general knowledge and cannot find the line in the text.

notes: E edit: Audio cannot hold a finger pointing at the text; have the child read the line out, and the recording holds all of it.

before.statement: Reads a grade-level passage aloud and answers a question whose answer is stated in the text.
before.adult_sees: The educator hears the reading and sees the child point to where the text says it.
before.counter_example: Answers from general knowledge without pointing to where the text says it.

behaviours.statement: Explains a science or geography fact just taught in their own words, with a because.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator hears the fact restated differently from the book, with a reason attached.
behaviours.counter_example: Repeats the textbook sentence word for word.

behaviours.statement: Measures a length or a volume with the right tool and records it with its unit.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the tool chosen fit the quantity and the unit written beside the number.
behaviours.counter_example: Writes a number without a unit or with the wrong tool's unit.

behaviours.statement: Completes a short timed practice set within the time allotted to them and re-works one answer in the margin before handing in.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the set finished within the child's allotted time and one answer worked a second time in the margin.
behaviours.counter_example: Finishes early and sits with the sheet untouched until time is called.

notes: R edit: 'In the time given' fixes one limit for all; a child with an agreed extra-time accommodation must be able to earn this within their own time.
D edit: 'Checks one answer' is invisible unless it leaves a mark; a tick or a correction on the sheet is what two educators can both see.
E edit: With thirty sheets I cannot see a child 'check' an answer; a re-worked answer in the margin is visible to any colleague.
chair edit: merged: the educator's visible re-working in the margin with the rights seat's allotted time (accommodations).

before.statement: Completes a short timed set of practice questions in the time given and checks one answer before handing in.
before.adult_sees: The educator sees the set finished in time and one answer visibly re-checked.
before.counter_example: Finishes early and hands in without looking back at any answer.

behaviours.statement: Writes a paragraph of four or more sentences on one topic, with a first sentence that says what it is about.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator reads a first sentence that announces the topic and sentences that stay on it.
behaviours.counter_example: Writes four sentences on four different things.

behaviours.statement: Reads a short passage aloud in a taught language that is not their home language and answers one question in it.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator hears the reading and the answer both in that language, in its lesson.
behaviours.counter_example: Sounds out the passage correctly, then gives the answer in the language they speak at home.

notes: chair add: educator: the cell was English and maths only; in a Pune school a second and third language take a third of the timetable. The founders decide which languages and from which stage. Revised on the seats' second look: development: anchored on a language that is not the child's home language, so one line measures one thing.

behaviours.statement: Asks a question in a lesson that names the exact part they did not understand.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator hears the question point to one step, one word or one line, not to the whole topic.
behaviours.counter_example: Asks the educator to explain the whole topic again from the start.

notes: chair add: parent: the profile's own 'I don't know how to solve this yet' had no line in this capability; the cell was six curriculum checks. Revised on the seats' second look: rights: the counter no longer pictures the lost child; the look-alike is the whole-topic question.

behaviours.statement: Solves a problem needing three or more steps, laying out each step so another student could follow it.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator can follow the working from the first step to the answer without asking.
behaviours.counter_example: Reaches the right answer with steps missing or out of order.

behaviours.statement: Summarises a textbook chapter in ten sentences that keep its main claims and drop its examples.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator reads claims in the child's words and no copied examples.
behaviours.counter_example: Copies the chapter's first sentences in order.

behaviours.statement: Uses a subject's technical term correctly in an explanation, and gives a plain-words version when asked.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator hears the term fit its meaning and a plain version follow on request.
behaviours.counter_example: Uses the term correctly in a rehearsed sentence and cannot give a plain-words version when asked.

notes: D edit: The over-count is parroting, the term used correctly by rote; the draft's counter is a plain failure, not a look-alike.

before.counter_example: Uses the term in a sentence that does not fit its meaning.

behaviours.statement: Records an experiment's method, readings and result in a table, with units, on the day it is done.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the table filled during the practical, units included.
behaviours.counter_example: Writes the expected result before taking the readings.

behaviours.statement: Sits a full-period written test under exam rules and attempts every question, showing working where asked.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees every question attempted and working where the paper asks for it.
behaviours.counter_example: Leaves the last questions blank with time remaining.

behaviours.statement: Writes an essay of several paragraphs that explains a process or event using facts from the unit.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator reads paragraphs that each carry a different part of the explanation.
behaviours.counter_example: Writes several paragraphs that restate one point.

behaviours.statement: Volunteers to work through their own wrong answer on the board with the class, saying where it went wrong.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator hears the offer come from the child, then sees them at the board pointing to the step that went wrong.
behaviours.counter_example: Works through the wrong answer at the board because the educator called them up.

notes: chair add: parent: the school's meaning of unafraid, a wrong answer treated as information in front of others, had no line in this capability. Revised on the seats' second look: development and rights, independently: the offer must come from the child; being sent to the board is exposure, not courage.

behaviours.statement: Solves an unseen problem in the board's format by choosing which method applies, and writes one line on why that method.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator reads a method that fits the problem and a written line giving the reason for choosing it.
behaviours.counter_example: Applies the method just practised whether or not it fits.

notes: D edit: Captured as a test, so 'says why' cannot be heard; the reason must be written to be evidence.
E edit: In a test nobody speaks; 'says why' cannot be captured under exam rules, so the reason must be written on the paper.
chair edit: educator and development seats, identical: in a test nobody speaks, so the reason is written.

before.statement: Solves an unseen problem in the board's format by choosing which method applies, and says why that method.
before.adult_sees: The educator sees a method chosen to fit the problem and a reason given for the choice.

behaviours.statement: Reads a primary source or a research abstract and states its claim and its evidence separately.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the claim and the evidence written as two separate things.
behaviours.counter_example: Summarises the source's topic without separating claim from evidence.

behaviours.statement: Teaches a concept from their own subject to a younger student, using two different explanations.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator hears the second explanation differ from the first when the first does not land, and notes it without the younger child's name.
behaviours.counter_example: Reads their notes aloud to the younger student.

notes: R edit: A video puts a younger child, who gave no consent, into another child's ten-year record; the educator hears both explanations directly, and the note carries no other child's name.
D edit: Two explanations heard is an observation note; a video of a younger child is heavier than the evidence needs.
E edit: A note that the second explanation differed from the first holds this; filming a younger child's lesson is heavy and not the lightest mode.

before.adult_sees: The educator hears the second explanation differ from the first when the first does not land.

behaviours.statement: Derives a formula or result from first principles on paper, rather than quoting it.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the derivation start from definitions, not from the formula.
behaviours.counter_example: Quotes the formula and substitutes numbers.

behaviours.statement: Completes a full board-pattern examination under exam conditions, managing time across all sections.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees every section attempted within the time.
behaviours.counter_example: Runs out of time with a whole section unattempted.

behaviours.statement: Writes an extended piece that argues a position using sources cited by name.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees named sources and a position that rests on them.
behaviours.counter_example: Lists sources at the end that the argument itself never uses.

notes: P edit: 'an invented one' accuses my child of fabricating a source; the near-miss an educator meets is sources listed but never used.

before.counter_example: Asserts a position with no source or with an invented one.

capabilities.name: Thinking & reasoning
capabilities.observable_at_16: Defines problems, evaluates evidence, reasons quantitatively and changes position when evidence warrants.

behaviours.statement: Asks a why question about something just seen or heard, such as why the ice melted.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator hears a why that follows from the moment, not from a book.
behaviours.counter_example: Asks 'why' again to each answer without waiting to hear it, as a way of keeping the adult talking.

notes: D edit: The over-count at three to five is the serial 'why' that ignores the answer; the draft's counter names a different, rarer confusion.

before.counter_example: Asks a question the educator has just answered.

behaviours.statement: Says what will happen before a simple test, such as which object will sink, and then checks.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator hears the prediction before the object touches the water.
behaviours.counter_example: Says the answer after seeing the result.

behaviours.statement: Gives a reason for a choice when asked, such as why this block goes on the bottom.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator hears a reason that refers to the block, not just to wanting it.
behaviours.counter_example: Says 'because' and repeats the choice.

behaviours.statement: Points out one way two things are the same and one way they differ.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator hears both a likeness and a difference named.
behaviours.counter_example: Names only what each thing is.

behaviours.statement: Changes a guess after seeing a result that does not match it, and says so.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator hears the child say the guess was wrong and give the new one.
behaviours.counter_example: Repeats the first guess after seeing the result.

behaviours.statement: Says which of two events happened first and which one made the other happen, in a story or a game.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator hears the order and the cause both stated.
behaviours.counter_example: Lists both events without saying which caused which.

notes: E edit: Audio in circle time is not realistic with thirty children; a note that the order and the cause were both stated holds it.

behaviours.statement: Turns a wondering into a question that can be tested in class, such as does the plant grow faster near the window.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator hears a question the class could actually set up and answer.
behaviours.counter_example: Asks a question no one in the room could test.

behaviours.statement: Writes a prediction before an investigation and the result after, and states whether they matched.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the prediction dated before the result.
behaviours.counter_example: Writes the prediction after the result is known.

behaviours.statement: Backs a claim with one piece of evidence from something read, measured or observed.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator hears or reads the evidence named beside the claim.
behaviours.counter_example: Backs a claim with 'everyone knows'.

behaviours.statement: Spots a pattern in a table or chart, such as one column larger in every row, and says what it might mean.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator hears the pattern described and a meaning offered.
behaviours.counter_example: Reads single values from the chart without a pattern.

notes: D edit: The behaviour is spoken ('says what it might mean'; the adult hears); an artefact holds the chart, not the reasoning.
E edit: The evidence is what the child says about the chart, not the chart; a note holds the words, an artefact does not.

behaviours.statement: Changes an answer after new evidence and writes the reason for the change beside it.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the old answer, the new one and the reason, all visible.
behaviours.counter_example: Rubs out the first answer so the change is invisible.

behaviours.statement: Sorts statements about a topic into facts and opinions and explains one sorting.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the sort and hears one placement justified.
behaviours.counter_example: Sorts by whether the statement agrees with their own view.

behaviours.statement: Designs a fair test with one thing changed and the rest kept the same, and names what is kept the same.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees one variable changed and the controls listed.
behaviours.counter_example: Changes two things at once and reports a result.

behaviours.statement: Judges whether a source is trustworthy by who wrote it, when and why, before using it.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the author, date and purpose noted before the source is cited.
behaviours.counter_example: Uses the first search result without saying who wrote it.

behaviours.statement: Estimates the size of an answer before calculating and writes whether the calculated result agrees with the estimate.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the estimate written above the working and a tick or a note comparing it with the answer.
behaviours.counter_example: Writes an estimate after the calculation that matches the answer exactly.

notes: D edit: As drafted it can only be recorded when an error happens to occur; comparing the result with the estimate is observable every time.
E edit: As written I can only record it on the day an error happens to occur; the estimate and the comparison are visible on every sheet.
chair edit: both seats: the comparison is observable every time, not only when an error happens; development's statement and counter, educator's concrete adult_sees.

before.statement: Estimates the size of an answer before calculating and uses the estimate to catch an error.
before.adult_sees: The educator sees the estimate written first and an error caught by it.
before.counter_example: Calculates first and accepts any answer.

behaviours.statement: Names an assumption in an argument, their own or another's, and says what changes if it is false.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator hears the assumption named and its consequence traced.
behaviours.counter_example: Restates the argument's conclusion and calls it the assumption.

notes: D edit: The actual confusion is a conclusion mistaken for an assumption; 'just an opinion' is unrelated to the behaviour.

before.counter_example: Labels a disagreement as 'just an opinion'.

behaviours.statement: Concedes a point in a discussion when the other side's evidence is stronger, and says which evidence moved them.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator hears the concession and the evidence named.
behaviours.counter_example: Says 'fine, you win' to end the exchange without naming any evidence.

notes: D edit: Social surrender looks like concession; the discrimination observers need is evidence named versus argument abandoned.

before.counter_example: Goes quiet rather than saying which point stood.

behaviours.statement: Puts a number on a claim, such as how much faster, and says how it was measured.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the number and the measurement it rests on.
behaviours.counter_example: Says 'much faster' without a measurement.

behaviours.statement: Writes a problem statement that says what is known, what is asked and what would count as solved, before starting.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the statement written before any working.
behaviours.counter_example: Starts computing before saying what the question is.

behaviours.statement: Weighs two sources that disagree and explains in writing which to trust more and why.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator reads both sources named and a reasoned choice between them.
behaviours.counter_example: Picks the source that agrees with their first view.

behaviours.statement: Checks a result by a second method or by trying an extreme case, and reports the check alongside the answer.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the second method or the extreme case written beside the answer.
behaviours.counter_example: Reports the answer with a note that it 'seems right'.

notes: P edit: 'limiting case' is a mathematician's phrase; 'an extreme case' says the same to a parent at first reading.

before.statement: Checks a result by a second method or a limiting case and reports the check alongside the answer.
before.adult_sees: The educator sees the second method or the limiting case beside the answer.

behaviours.statement: Uses a model or a formula to predict a case not yet seen, then compares with a measurement.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the prediction made before the measurement and the comparison after.
behaviours.counter_example: Fits a model to data already seen and stops.

behaviours.statement: Records a change of position on a question in writing, stating the evidence that changed it.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator reads the earlier position, the later one and the evidence between.
behaviours.counter_example: Presents the final position as if it had been held from the start.

behaviours.statement: Identifies the specific flaw in a flawed argument, such as a sample too small or a cause confused with a correlation.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator reads the flaw named precisely in the child's written response, such as the sample size or cause confused with correlation.
behaviours.counter_example: Calls the argument 'wrong' without naming the flaw.

notes: D edit: Capture is artefact but adult_sees says 'hears'; align them so the record is the written naming of the flaw.
E edit: The draft says I hear the flaw but files an artefact; in a class discussion the note is the capture, in an exercise the page.
chair edit: artefact kept: the record is the written naming of the flaw, which a second reader can check; the development seat's adult_sees aligns with it.

before.adult_sees: The educator hears the flaw named precisely.

capabilities.name: Learning & agency
capabilities.observable_at_16: Sets goals, researches independently, seeks feedback, reflects and improves.

behaviours.statement: Chooses an activity with an end point, such as a puzzle or a painting, at free-choice time and stays with it to the end.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the activity chosen unprompted and the puzzle completed or the painting declared done by the child.
behaviours.counter_example: Finishes an activity the educator assigned rather than one they chose themselves.

notes: R edit: The counter describes flitting 'each time an adult looks away': attention by paraphrase and a motive read into a small child; the look-alike is a finished but assigned activity.
D edit: 'Finished' has no agreed meaning for open block play; anchoring on activities with a natural end gives two observers the same stopping point.
P edit: 'each time an adult looks away' paints a three-year-old as sneaky; the honest near-miss is staying only while the educator sits there.
chair edit: rights seat's counter: the distinctive feature is the child's own choice, so the look-alike is finishing an assigned activity.

before.counter_example: Moves to a new activity each time an adult looks away.
before.statement: Chooses an activity at free-choice time and stays with it until it is finished.
before.adult_sees: The educator sees the activity chosen unprompted and brought to an end.

behaviours.statement: Tries a task on their own first and then asks for help with the specific part that is hard.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees an attempt before the request and hears the hard part named.
behaviours.counter_example: Asks for help before touching the task.

behaviours.statement: Tells an adult one thing they learned or could do today that they could not do before.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator hears a learning named, not an activity listed.
behaviours.counter_example: Names an activity done today without what was learned.

notes: R edit: A recording of a child under eight is identifiable data needing verifiable parental consent (DPDP Act; verify detail), kept ten years; the educator's note of the words holds this.
E edit: Recording each child's voice in an end-of-day circle is not realistic; a note quoting the one thing named holds it.

behaviours.statement: Fixes a mistake in their own work after one hint, without the adult doing it for them.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator gives one hint and sees the child make the correction.
behaviours.counter_example: Waits for the adult to correct it.

behaviours.statement: Puts materials back where they belong so the next child can use them, without being told.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the materials returned to their place unprompted.
behaviours.counter_example: Puts materials away only when asked by name.

notes: D skip: Care of shared materials is not learning or agency and duplicates keeps-a-shared-space-tidy under society; give the slot a learning behaviour (see missing).

chair accept: the development seat would move care of materials to society; the educator and parent found the society row the duplicate, and 'without being told' is the agency. One owner: learning-and-agency.

behaviours.statement: Tries again, in the same session, at something that failed the first time, such as a tower or a jump.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the second attempt follow the first failure.
behaviours.counter_example: Tries again after an adult says 'try once more'.

notes: D edit: The over-count is the prompted retry; leaving the activity is a non-example, not a look-alike.

before.counter_example: Leaves the activity after the first failure.

behaviours.statement: Names something they want to learn to do, such as tying laces or writing a letter, and asks to be shown.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator hears the wish named and the request to be shown, unprompted.
behaviours.counter_example: Agrees to learn what the educator proposes.

notes: chair add: development: goal-setting had no seed at this stage; a self-named skill is its four-to-seven-year form.

behaviours.statement: Writes one learning goal for the week in their own words and marks on Friday whether it was met.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator reads a goal in the child's words and sees it reviewed on Friday.
behaviours.counter_example: Copies the class goal from the board.

notes: E edit: 'Checks it off or not' is unclear; say what I record: the Friday mark against a goal written on Monday.

before.statement: Writes one learning goal for the week, in their own words, and checks it off or not on Friday.

behaviours.statement: Looks up an answer in a book, chart or dictionary before asking the educator.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the resource opened before the hand goes up.
behaviours.counter_example: Asks the educator the spelling of a word on the word wall.

behaviours.statement: Names, in a reflection, what was hard about a task and one thing to do differently next time.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator reads or hears a specific difficulty and a specific change, and notes that both were named rather than filing the words.
behaviours.counter_example: Writes 'it was easy' or 'it was hard' without a why.

notes: R edit: A child's recorded words about what they find hard, filed ten years, become a self-written deficit record; note that a difficulty and a change were named, not the words.
E edit: Grade 3-5 reflections are written in the notebook; the page is the lightest capture, not a voice recording of each child.
chair edit: rights seat's mode: the record holds that a difficulty and a change were named, not the child's words; the notebook page stays the child's.

before.adult_sees: The educator reads or hears a specific difficulty and a specific change.

behaviours.statement: Uses a written comment from the educator to change the next draft, and can point to the change.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the commented point changed in the next draft.
behaviours.counter_example: Rewrites the draft without touching the point commented on.

behaviours.statement: Keeps their own record of practice sheets done and skills mastered, and updates it unprompted.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the record current without having asked.
behaviours.counter_example: Fills the record only when the educator checks it.

behaviours.statement: Chooses the Hard or Advance version of a task when offered a choice of difficulty, and attempts it.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the Hard or Advance sheet taken from the choice offered and worked on.
behaviours.counter_example: Chooses the harder version and hands it in blank.

notes: E edit: The school's difficulty words are Easy, Medium, Hard and Advance; use them so every educator means the same thing by 'harder'.

before.statement: Chooses the harder version of a task when offered a choice, and attempts it.
before.adult_sees: The educator sees the harder version taken and worked on.

behaviours.statement: Breaks a multi-week project into dated steps at the start and shows, at a check-in, the steps done so far ticked.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the plan dated from the start of the project, with the steps completed so far ticked, at a check-in.
behaviours.counter_example: Writes the plan on the last day.

notes: E edit: 'As the weeks pass' is not one occasion; the record is a check-in where the dated plan shows which steps are ticked.

before.statement: Breaks a multi-week project into steps with dates and ticks them off as they are done.
before.adult_sees: The educator sees the plan dated at the start and ticked as the weeks pass.

behaviours.statement: Finds two sources on a topic without help and notes where each was found.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees two sources located by the child and their origins noted.
behaviours.counter_example: Notes two sources that were both handed to them by the educator.

notes: P edit: 'cites it as two' accuses a twelve-year-old of faking a bibliography; the honest near-miss is two sources that someone else found.

before.counter_example: Uses one source and cites it as two.

behaviours.statement: Asks a peer or educator for feedback on one named aspect of their work before it is due.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator hears the aspect named in the request.
behaviours.counter_example: Asks 'is this good?' about the whole piece.

behaviours.statement: Marks their own work against the rubric before submitting and notes where it falls short.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the self-marking with at least one shortfall named.
behaviours.counter_example: Awards full marks on every line.

behaviours.statement: Reads their own skill map, names a gap, and chooses practice for it.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the gap named and the practice chosen to match it.
behaviours.counter_example: Practises only skills already secure.

behaviours.statement: Keeps working on a problem after a first attempt fails, trying a different approach within the session.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees a second, different approach follow the failed one.
behaviours.counter_example: Repeats the same failed approach three times.

behaviours.statement: Completes an independent study from question to finished product and shows the milestones they set with the date each was met.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the finished study and, beside it, the child's own milestones with the dates they were met.
behaviours.counter_example: Presents the product with a plan written in the final week.

notes: D edit: 'Over a term, meeting milestones' is a pattern, not an occasion; the moment is the presentation with the dated plan, which also separates it from creation's investigation.
E edit: A term is not one occasion; the record is the finished study with the child's own dated milestones beside it.
chair edit: both seats: a term is a pattern; the occasion is the finished study shown with the dated milestones. Educator's statement, development's counter.

before.statement: Carries an independent study from a question to a finished product over a term, meeting their own milestones.
before.adult_sees: The educator sees milestones set by the child and met through the term.
before.counter_example: Completes the study in the last week.

behaviours.statement: Reviews their own bibliography and drops or replaces an unreliable source, saying why.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees a source removed and the reason recorded.
behaviours.counter_example: Adds sources to lengthen the list.

behaviours.statement: Seeks feedback from an expert outside school, found by the child or introduced by the school and known to it, and reports what they learned.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator knows who was approached and how, and sees the expert's feedback and the change it led to.
behaviours.counter_example: Reports the feedback without any change made.

notes: R edit: A minor approaching an outside adult must go through a contact the school knows (safeguarding), and the school should offer such contacts so this does not depend on family networks.
P edit: As written it rewards the child whose family knows an expert; say the school may make the introduction so every child can earn this line.
chair edit: merged: the parent's school-introduced expert with the rights seat's contact the school knows.

before.statement: Seeks feedback from someone outside school with relevant expertise and reports what they learned from it.
before.adult_sees: The educator sees the expert's feedback and the change it led to.

behaviours.statement: States a standard for their work above the rubric's, and shows where the work meets it.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator reads a standard the rubric did not ask for and sees it met.
behaviours.counter_example: Restates the rubric as their standard.

behaviours.statement: Learns an unfamiliar tool or topic from documentation or a course on their own, and demonstrates it.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the tool used or the topic applied, not described.
behaviours.counter_example: Watches a tutorial and describes it without using the tool.

notes: D edit: The evidence is a demonstration the educator watches; a note holds it, video is heavier than needed.
E edit: Seeing the tool used or the topic applied is an observation; a clip adds nothing a dated note does not hold.

behaviours.statement: Returns to a piece of work after a public setback, such as a lost debate or a failed demonstration, and improves it.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the work taken up again and changed after the setback.
behaviours.counter_example: Drops the piece after the setback.

capabilities.name: Creation & problem solving
capabilities.observable_at_16: Turns ideas into experiments, prototypes, designs, investigations and useful outputs.

behaviours.statement: Builds something with blocks or junk that matches a plan said aloud beforehand.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator hears the plan first and sees the build match it.
behaviours.counter_example: Names what the finished pile is after building it.

behaviours.statement: Solves a practical problem, such as a bridge that falls, by changing the materials or the design.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the change made by the child and the bridge stand.
behaviours.counter_example: Asks an adult to fix the bridge.

behaviours.statement: Draws a picture that shows an idea or a plan and explains what each part is.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator hears each part of the drawing named for what it does.
behaviours.counter_example: Draws and says it is 'just a drawing'.

behaviours.statement: Invents a new rule for a familiar game and plays a round with it.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator hears the rule proposed before play and sees it kept.
behaviours.counter_example: Proposes a new rule and then plays the round by the old rules.

notes: R edit: 'Changes rules mid-game to win' reads a motive into a small child and files cheating as the contrast; the look-alike is a rule announced but not played.
P edit: 'to win' reads a four-year-old's motive and calls them a cheat; the near-miss is a rule announced after the round has started.
chair edit: rights seat's counter: a rule proposed but not played is the near-miss; both seats removed the motive.

before.counter_example: Changes rules mid-game to win.

behaviours.statement: Makes a second version of something made, and says what is different.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees two versions and hears the difference named.
behaviours.counter_example: Makes the same thing again.

behaviours.statement: Uses a simple tool, such as scissors, a hole punch or a magnifier, for its purpose without help.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the tool used as intended with no hand over hand.
behaviours.counter_example: Holds the tool and asks an adult to use it.

behaviours.statement: Makes something for a particular person, such as a card or a model, and gives it to them saying who it is for.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the thing handed over and hears who it is for.
behaviours.counter_example: Makes a card because the whole class was asked to make one.

notes: chair add: parent: creation had no kind line at any stage; making for someone else is the earliest form a parent would recognise.

behaviours.statement: Uses one object as another in pretend play, such as a block as a phone, and shows or tells what it stands for.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the object used as something else and the child make plain, by word or action, what it is now.
behaviours.counter_example: Uses a toy phone as a phone.

notes: chair add: development: symbolic substitution is the three-to-five-year-old's core creative act and the only creation behaviour a three-year-old can reliably show. Revised on the seats' second look: rights: 'shows or tells', so a child playing alone or without speech can show it.

behaviours.statement: Makes a model or device that does what it was meant to do, such as a lever that lifts a load.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the model do its job.
behaviours.counter_example: Presents a model that looks right and does not work.

behaviours.statement: Tests a design, records what failed and changes one thing before testing again.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the failure recorded and one change made.
behaviours.counter_example: Changes everything after a failure.

behaviours.statement: Writes a materials list and a step plan before making something, and follows it.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the list and plan written first and the make follow them.
behaviours.counter_example: Writes the list after making.

behaviours.statement: Writes an original story of their own with a beginning, a problem and an ending.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator reads a plot of the child's own with all three parts.
behaviours.counter_example: Retells a known story with the names changed.

notes: E edit: A poem has no 'problem and ending'; two educators would disagree over a poem. Keep the sentence to a story.

before.statement: Writes an original story or poem with a beginning, a problem and an ending.

behaviours.statement: Presents a made thing to the class and says what changed from the first version and why.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator hears the change and its reason.
behaviours.counter_example: Shows the thing without saying what was changed.

notes: D edit: The evidence is a change and its reason spoken; an observation note holds that, video adds nothing two educators need.
E edit: Hearing the change and its reason is a note; filming every child's show-and-tell in a class of thirty is not the lightest mode.

behaviours.statement: Chooses the right tool for a job from several available, and says why that one.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator hears the reason for the tool chosen.
behaviours.counter_example: Uses whatever tool is nearest.

behaviours.statement: Builds a prototype that meets a written brief with constraints, such as a budget or a size limit.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator checks the prototype against each constraint in the brief.
behaviours.counter_example: Builds something impressive that ignores the constraints.

behaviours.statement: Keeps an iteration log across several tests with what changed and what the results were.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator reads several entries, each with a change and a result.
behaviours.counter_example: Records the final version only.

behaviours.statement: Fixes a program of their own when a test input breaks it, and shows the failing input and the change made.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the input that broke the program and the line changed to fix it.
behaviours.counter_example: Deletes the failing test input so the program passes.

notes: D skip: Coding is already technology's middle-stage evidence (writes-a-text-program-with-a-loop-and-a-condition); one program would be filed twice. Keep it there.
E edit: The evidence is the fix happening when an input breaks it, which I watch; the code alone does not show it, and this separates it from technology's program line.
chair edit: the same program as writes-a-text-program-with-a-loop-and-a-condition under technology; re-worded to the act creation adds, fixing it when a test input breaks it.

before.statement: Writes a program that solves a set task, and fixes it when a test input breaks it.
before.adult_sees: The educator sees the program fail on an input and be fixed by the child.
before.counter_example: Copies a program and cannot change it when it breaks.

behaviours.statement: Produces a piece of art, media or performance for a real audience outside the class, such as younger children or parents.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the piece reach the audience it was made for.
behaviours.counter_example: Makes the piece for the class display only.

notes: chair edit: writing for an audience is writes-for-a-named-audience under communication; creation keeps art, media and performance.

before.statement: Produces a piece of writing, art or media for a real audience outside the class, such as younger children or parents.
before.adult_sees: The educator sees the piece reach its audience.
before.counter_example: Produces a piece only the educator sees.

behaviours.statement: Pitches a solution to a problem and names one trade-off it makes.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator hears the trade-off named in the pitch.
behaviours.counter_example: Pitches the solution as having no downside.

notes: D edit: A named trade-off is heard once and noted; video is heavier than the evidence.
E edit: A note that the trade-off was named holds this; video is heavy for a routine class pitch.

behaviours.statement: Carries out an investigation of an open question with a method they designed, and reports what was found.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees a method of the child's own and a finding, expected or not.
behaviours.counter_example: Follows a worksheet method and reports the expected answer.

behaviours.statement: Makes or repairs something that someone in the school asked for, and hands it over working.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the person who asked receive it and use it.
behaviours.counter_example: Makes something to a brief the educator set for marks.

notes: chair add: parent: a make that answers someone's real need is creation in the school's second word, and the capability never recorded one.

behaviours.statement: Makes an original artwork, composition or performance piece to a set theme and explains one choice made in it.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the piece and hears one choice in it explained.
behaviours.counter_example: Copies a piece found online and explains the theme.

notes: chair add: development: the arts vanished after the preparatory story or poem; creation at 11 to 14 is more than prototypes and code.

behaviours.statement: Delivers a project to a brief from someone outside school and incorporates their feedback.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the outside brief, the delivery and the feedback acted on.
behaviours.counter_example: Delivers to their own brief.

behaviours.statement: Documents a build or an experiment so another student repeats it without asking questions.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees another student repeat it from the document alone.
behaviours.counter_example: Documents it so only they can repeat it.

behaviours.statement: Builds a piece of software with tests, and shows a test catching a bug.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees a test fail on a bug and pass after the fix.
behaviours.counter_example: Shows working software with no tests.

behaviours.statement: Finishes a piece of work to exhibition standard and labels it with what it is and what changed from the first version.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the finished piece and its label naming the change from the first version.
behaviours.counter_example: Shows the first version with a label saying it is finished.

notes: D edit: As drafted it duplicates communication's presents-to-an-outside-audience; the creation-specific act is revising the work after public response.
E edit: As drafted it is the same moment as presents-to-an-outside-audience; make it about the made piece, and a note holds it.
chair edit: the same moment as presents-to-an-outside-audience under communication; re-worded to the act creation adds, finishing the work to exhibition standard.

before.statement: Exhibits or performs a piece of work publicly and answers questions about it.
before.adult_sees: The educator sees the work shown and questions taken.
before.counter_example: Exhibits the work and leaves before questions.

behaviours.statement: Completes a real task in a school-arranged and supervised internship or apprenticeship placement, confirmed by the host.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the host's confirmation of a task done, at a placement the school vetted and supervises.
behaviours.counter_example: Attends the placement without a completed task.

notes: R edit: Placements for 14–16-year-olds need school vetting of the host, supervision and hours limits (adolescent-labour rules; verify), and must not depend on which families have contacts.

before.statement: Completes a real task in an internship or apprenticeship placement, confirmed by the host.
before.adult_sees: The educator sees the host's confirmation of a task done.

behaviours.statement: Designs and runs an original investigation, from question to method to findings, and presents it.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the question, method and findings all the child's own.
behaviours.counter_example: Repeats a textbook investigation.

could_not.detail: Secondary behaviours assume placements, exhibitions and outside briefs that the school has not yet defined; they should be read as what the programme must make possible.

capabilities.name: Communication & collaboration
capabilities.observable_at_16: Writes, speaks, presents, listens, negotiates and contributes reliably to teams.

behaviours.statement: Tells the circle something that happened, in two or more connected sentences in a language they speak, so that listeners can follow.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator hears two connected sentences about one piece of news, in whichever language the child uses, with no prompt between them.
behaviours.counter_example: Says one word and stops when asked more.

notes: R edit: Audio of a small child's news files home life for ten years, and 'full sentences' must not mean English only; the educator's note holds the two connected sentences.
E edit: Audio in circle time is not realistic, and I cannot judge 'the circle follows'; two connected sentences with no prompt between them I can.
P edit: The evidence is two connected sentences, not what the news was; an audio file of my child's home news, kept ten years, is more than the school needs.
chair edit: merged: the educator's no prompt between the sentences with the rights seat's whichever language the child uses.

before.statement: Tells the circle a piece of news in two or more full sentences that others can follow.
before.adult_sees: The educator hears two connected sentences and sees the circle follow.

behaviours.statement: Listens to a classmate and says something back about what they said.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator hears the response refer to the classmate's words.
behaviours.counter_example: Waits for their own turn without responding.

behaviours.statement: Asks to join a game, and accepts a no or joins in the way agreed.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the ask and the answer respected.
behaviours.counter_example: Pushes into the game without asking.

behaviours.statement: Takes turns in a pair task, such as passing the crayon, without an adult managing it.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the turns pass with no adult counting.
behaviours.counter_example: Takes turns only when an adult counts.

notes: chair skip: one turn taken, two rows: waits-for-a-turn-without-a-reminder under self-and-relationships records the same act.

behaviours.statement: Shows a drawing or a build to the class and explains what it is.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator hears the explanation reach the class.
behaviours.counter_example: Holds up the work silently.

behaviours.statement: Uses words or signs to settle a dispute over a toy or a turn, such as proposing a swap.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator hears or sees the proposal made and sees the dispute end.
behaviours.counter_example: Repeats 'give it to me' louder until the other child gives in.

notes: R edit: 'Words' shuts out a signing or non-speaking child, and a counter naming grabbing or hitting invites an incident note into a capability file; the look-alike is words without a proposal.
E edit: Grabbing does not look like using words; the confusion I actually make is a child who uses words to wear the other down.
P edit: 'Grabs or hits' is not a look-alike, it is an accusation a parent will read; the near-miss is the dispute ending with no words used.
chair edit: educator's counter: the confusion an educator actually makes; both seats removed the incident wording.

before.statement: Uses words to settle a dispute over a toy or a turn, such as proposing a swap.
before.adult_sees: The educator hears the proposal and sees the dispute end.
before.counter_example: Grabs or hits to settle the dispute.

behaviours.statement: Gives a two-minute prepared talk to the class with a beginning and an end.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator hears a shaped talk delivered to the room.
behaviours.counter_example: Reads the talk from the page without looking up.

notes: E edit: Thirty talks a term cannot all be filmed; a note that the talk had a beginning and an end holds this.

behaviours.statement: Adds to a classmate's idea in discussion, naming whose idea it builds on.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator hears the classmate credited and the idea extended.
behaviours.counter_example: Repeats the classmate's idea in other words without adding to it.

notes: P edit: 'as their own' accuses an eight-year-old of stealing an idea; repeating it without adding anything is the honest near-miss.

before.counter_example: Presents the classmate's idea as their own.

behaviours.statement: Agrees roles with a group before a task starts and takes the role agreed.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the roles agreed first and kept.
behaviours.counter_example: Takes the role they want and leaves the rest.

behaviours.statement: Writes a letter or message to a real person for a purpose, such as a request or a thank you.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator reads a named recipient and a clear purpose.
behaviours.counter_example: Writes a letter to no one in particular.

behaviours.statement: Explains their method to a classmate who is stuck, without giving the answer.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator hears the method explained and the answer withheld.
behaviours.counter_example: Tells the classmate the answer.

behaviours.statement: Disagrees with a classmate's answer by giving a reason that addresses the answer, not the classmate, and lets the classmate reply.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator hears the disagreement and its reason addressed to the answer, not to the classmate, and the classmate given the floor.
behaviours.counter_example: Says 'you're wrong' without a reason.

notes: R edit: 'Politely' and 'without heat' judge manner and mood, which differ by culture and neurotype and are read into the child; the observable is a reason given and a reply allowed.
D edit: 'Politely' is a rating word observers score differently; a reason aimed at the answer rather than the person is what both can hear.
chair edit: merged: 'politely' and 'without heat' judge manner (rights, development); the observable is a reason about the answer and the classmate allowed to reply.

before.statement: Disagrees with a classmate's answer politely, giving a reason.
before.adult_sees: The educator hears the disagreement and its reason, without heat.

behaviours.statement: Presents to an audience using a visual aid they made, and answers a question from the floor.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the aid used and a question answered.
behaviours.counter_example: Reads slides aloud and takes no questions.

notes: E edit: A note that the aid was used and a question answered holds this; a clip is not the lightest mode.

behaviours.statement: Leads a small-group discussion so that every member speaks, and summarises what was agreed.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees every member speak and hears the summary.
behaviours.counter_example: Speaks most and summarises their own view.

behaviours.statement: Resolves a disagreement in a group task by proposing an option both sides accept.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the option proposed and both sides carry on.
behaviours.counter_example: Gives way to the louder side so that the task can go on.

notes: R edit: A counter that names going to the educator teaches children that asking an adult costs them credit; safeguarding needs the opposite; the look-alike is giving way to end the argument.

before.counter_example: Reports the disagreement to the educator to settle.

behaviours.statement: Writes a piece in a tone suited to a named audience, such as a report for the head or a guide for Grade 3.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator reads a tone that fits the audience named.
behaviours.counter_example: Writes in the same tone for every audience.

notes: P edit: 'register' is a linguist's word; 'tone' says the same thing to a parent at first reading.

before.statement: Writes a piece in a register suited to a named audience, such as a report for the head or a guide for Grade 3.
before.adult_sees: The educator reads a register that fits the audience named.
before.counter_example: Writes in the same register for every audience.

behaviours.statement: Gives a classmate written feedback with one strength and one specific change to make.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator reads a strength and a change the classmate could act on.
behaviours.counter_example: Writes 'good job' or 'needs work'.

behaviours.statement: Argues the side assigned to them in a structured debate, using evidence for it, whichever side that is.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator hears evidence used for the assigned side and notes that the side was assigned.
behaviours.counter_example: Argues the assigned side with opinions and no evidence.

notes: R edit: 'A side they do not hold' makes the educator infer and file the child's beliefs; a video of a child arguing a view, kept ten years, reads as their own.
D edit: Refusing is a non-example; the over-count is a fluent assigned-side speech with nothing behind it.
P edit: A child who will not argue against their conscience must not be the not-evidence example parents read; the near-miss is a side argued without evidence.
chair edit: parent's counter: the near-miss is arguing without evidence; the rights seat's swap wording could still lead an educator to note the child's wish about sides.

before.statement: Argues an assigned side in a structured debate, including a side they do not hold, with evidence.
before.adult_sees: The educator hears evidence used for the assigned side.
before.counter_example: Refuses to argue a side they do not hold.

behaviours.statement: Presents work to an audience outside school, such as parents, a partner organisation or a competition panel, and handles questions.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the outside audience and questions handled.
behaviours.counter_example: Presents only to classmates.

behaviours.statement: Runs a meeting with an agenda and leaves it with actions assigned to named people.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator reads the agenda and the actions with names.
behaviours.counter_example: Holds a meeting with no record of what was decided.

behaviours.statement: Negotiates an outcome with adults, such as a change to a school routine, presenting a case and reaching an agreed outcome with them.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the case made, the adults' response answered, and an outcome both sides state as agreed.
behaviours.counter_example: Complains about the routine without proposing a case.

notes: R edit: 'Accepting conditions' makes compliance the evidence, so a child who argues the adults into a better outcome earns nothing; the observable is a case made and an agreement reached.

before.statement: Negotiates an outcome with adults, such as a change to a school routine, presenting a case and accepting conditions.
before.adult_sees: The educator sees the case made and conditions accepted.

behaviours.statement: Writes a formal document, such as a proposal, a report or an application, that a stranger could act on.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator gives the document to someone uninvolved and sees them act on it.
behaviours.counter_example: Writes a document that needs the author present to explain it.

behaviours.statement: Runs a mentoring session with a younger student, in a pairing the school set up, and adds it to a log of earlier dated sessions.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the session take place and the log with earlier dated entries, kept without the younger child's name or difficulties.
behaviours.counter_example: Logs a first meeting as mentoring.

notes: R edit: A standing older–younger pairing over weeks needs adult supervision (safeguarding), and the younger child's name and difficulties must not sit in the mentor's ten-year file.
D edit: 'Over several weeks' is a pattern, not one occasion; the session with its dated log is the moment an educator can record.
chair edit: merged: development's one session added to a dated log; rights' school-set pairing and no younger child's name or difficulties in the record.

before.statement: Mentors a younger student over several weeks and records what they worked on together.
before.adult_sees: The educator sees the record of sessions and what each covered.
before.counter_example: Meets the younger student once.

behaviours.statement: Restates an opposing view to its holder's satisfaction before answering it, in a discussion.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator hears the holder agree the restatement is fair.
behaviours.counter_example: Answers an opposing view without restating it.

could_not.detail: Word tags follow the draft meanings of capable, kind and unafraid in the proposal; if the founders' meanings differ, the tags should be re-read against them.

capabilities.name: Technology & AI
capabilities.observable_at_16: Uses digital tools productively; verifies AI outputs; understands bias, privacy, provenance and limitations.

behaviours.statement: Operates a simple screen-free device, such as a story player or a torch, for a stated purpose, with an adult present.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the device used for the purpose the child stated and put down afterwards.
behaviours.counter_example: Taps a device at random.

notes: E edit: The school has no screen below Grade 4 and a camera has a screen; name a screen-free device so nobody hands over a phone.
P edit: The school promises no screen below Grade 4; a parent reading 'photographing their work' will ask which promise holds, so say screen-free.
chair edit: parent's wording: plain words, a screen-free example a parent recognises; both seats agree on screen-free.

before.statement: Operates a simple device for a purpose, such as playing a recorded story or photographing their work, with an adult present.
before.adult_sees: The educator sees the device used for the stated purpose and put down after.

behaviours.statement: Follows a three-step sequence of instructions, given in a language they understand, in order, such as in a coding game played without a screen.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator gives the steps in a language the child understands and sees the three done in the order given.
behaviours.counter_example: Does the steps in a different order.

notes: R edit: As written, a child new to the school's language fails a sequencing behaviour for not understanding the words; the instructions must be in a language the child understands.
P edit: 'unplugged coding game' is staff-room talk; 'played without a screen' tells a parent of a five-year-old what they most want to know.
chair edit: merged: the parent's plain words for unplugged with the rights seat's language the child understands.

before.statement: Follows a three-step sequence of instructions in order, such as in an unplugged coding game.
before.adult_sees: The educator sees the three steps done in the order given.

behaviours.statement: Gives a classmate step-by-step instructions to move across a grid, and corrects one wrong step.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator hears the steps and sees one corrected.
behaviours.counter_example: Says 'go there' and points.

notes: P edit: Directing a classmate across a grid is not kindness in the founders' meaning; tagging it kind pads the kind column my child's report draws on.

behaviours.statement: Says whether a picture or a story is real or made up, and gives one reason.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator hears the judgement and a reason for it.
behaviours.counter_example: Says real or pretend without a reason.

notes: E edit: Audio in circle time is not realistic; a note of the judgement and the reason given holds it.

behaviours.statement: Asks before using a classmate's crayons, drawing or belongings.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator hears the ask before the crayons or the drawing are touched.
behaviours.counter_example: Asks only after already picking the thing up.

notes: E edit: Children below Grade 4 have no device at school; name what they actually have, or the line reads as if they do.
P edit: 'Takes it while the classmate is away' reads as theft against a four-year-old; asking after already picking it up is the honest near-miss.

before.statement: Asks before using a classmate's device, drawing or belongings.
before.adult_sees: The educator hears the ask before the object is touched.
before.counter_example: Takes it while the classmate is away.

behaviours.statement: Carries and puts away a shared device carefully, as shown.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the device carried with two hands and returned to its place.
behaviours.counter_example: Drops or leaves the device on the floor.

notes: R edit: 'Carried with two hands' excludes a child with a limb difference or a child using a walking aid; 'securely, as shown' is the observable that every child can meet.
E skip: Below Grade 4 there is no device to handle; what is left is putting shared materials back, already recorded under learning-and-agency.

chair skip: educator's skip stands: below Grade 4 there is no device to handle, and care of shared materials is already recorded under learning-and-agency (both the parent and the educator named the duplicate).

behaviours.statement: Uses a digital tool to produce a piece of work, such as a typed paragraph or a chart from data they collected.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the finished piece made with the tool.
behaviours.counter_example: Uses the tool to play during work time.

behaviours.statement: Writes a short block-based program and fixes it when it does not do what was intended.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the program misbehave and the child change it until it works.
behaviours.counter_example: Runs a sample program without changing it.

behaviours.statement: Explains in plain words what a short set of instructions or program will do before running it.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator hears the prediction before the run.
behaviours.counter_example: Runs it and then describes what happened.

behaviours.statement: Checks an answer from a search or an AI tool against a book or a second source before using it.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the second source opened before the answer is used.
behaviours.counter_example: Copies the first answer given.

behaviours.statement: Says what should not be shared online, such as full name, address or school, and applies it in a task.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the private fields left out in the task.
behaviours.counter_example: Types their full name and address into a form without asking.

behaviours.statement: Names where an image or fact came from when using it in their work.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the source named beside the image or fact.
behaviours.counter_example: Uses an image with no source.

behaviours.statement: Writes or dictates step-by-step instructions for a classmate to draw a figure, then changes a step when the drawing does not match what was meant.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the steps, the drawing they produced and the step rewritten after it; the filed artefact is the child's own instruction sheet, not the classmate's drawing.
behaviours.counter_example: Draws the figure for the classmate instead of rewriting the step.

notes: chair add: development: gives Grade 3, which has no screen, an observable algorithm behaviour and a genuine step from the foundational grid game. Revised on the seats' second look: rights: dictation admitted; the filed artefact is the child's own sheet, never the classmate's drawing.

behaviours.statement: Chooses a digital tool suited to a task, such as a spreadsheet for data, and justifies the choice.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator hears the justification and sees the tool fit.
behaviours.counter_example: Uses the same tool for everything.

behaviours.statement: Writes a text-based program with a loop and a condition that solves a set problem.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the loop and condition in the code and the problem solved.
behaviours.counter_example: Writes straight-line code with no loop.

behaviours.statement: Checks an AI tool's output claim by claim against a source, marking each claim confirmed or corrected and naming the source used.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees each claim marked confirmed or corrected and the source used written beside the marks.
behaviours.counter_example: Marks every claim confirmed without opening a source.

notes: D edit: As drafted it needs an error to exist; claim-by-claim checking against a source is observable on every occasion and is the actual skill.
E edit: As written it needs the tool to have erred that day; checking every claim against a source is visible whether or not it did.
chair edit: both seats: checking claim by claim is observable whether or not the tool erred; development's wording names the source.

before.statement: Uses an AI tool for a task and finds and corrects one error in its output, showing how it was checked.
before.adult_sees: The educator sees the error marked and the check that found it.
before.counter_example: Submits the AI output unchanged.

behaviours.statement: Explains, with an example, how an app's recommendation or an AI answer can be biased by its data.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator hears a concrete example, not a slogan.
behaviours.counter_example: Says 'AI is biased' without an example.

behaviours.statement: Sets privacy settings on a school account as taught and explains what each setting protects.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the settings set and hears each one explained.
behaviours.counter_example: Leaves defaults and cannot say what they do.

behaviours.statement: States where AI was used in their work and where it was not, when handing it in.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator reads the attribution on the submitted work.
behaviours.counter_example: Writes 'used AI' on the cover sheet with no indication of where.

notes: P edit: 'as fully their own' is a dishonesty charge a parent will read; the near-miss is an attribution too vague to use.

before.counter_example: Hands in AI-assisted work as fully their own.

behaviours.statement: Builds a working digital product, such as a website, app or automation, for a real user, and gets their feedback.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the user use it and the feedback recorded.
behaviours.counter_example: Builds a demo no one uses.

notes: D edit: The evidence is the user's recorded feedback; filming another person using it is heavier than needed and adds nothing to agreement.
E edit: The evidence is the product and the user's recorded feedback, both artefacts; a clip of someone using it is not the lightest mode.

behaviours.statement: Writes a program that reads real data, uses a ready-made code library, and produces a checked result.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the check that the result is right.
behaviours.counter_example: Produces output with no check that it is right.

notes: P edit: 'uses a library' means books to a parent; 'ready-made code library' is understood at first reading.

before.statement: Writes a program that reads real data, uses a library, and produces a checked result.

behaviours.statement: Uses AI in a piece of work with a log of prompts, what was kept, what was rejected and why.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator reads the log beside the work.
behaviours.counter_example: Keeps the prompts but not what was rejected or why.

notes: P edit: 'describes it as research' implies my child disguised the AI use; the honest near-miss is an incomplete log.

before.counter_example: Uses AI and describes it as 'research'.

behaviours.statement: Evaluates a technology's benefits and harms for a named group, with evidence, and takes a position.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator reads the weighing and the position taken.
behaviours.counter_example: Lists benefits and harms without weighing them.

behaviours.statement: Completes a task without AI that they could have done with it, and writes two lines on what doing it alone showed.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the task done unaided and reads the two lines beneath it.
behaviours.counter_example: Does the task unaided because AI was not allowed, and says nothing about what it showed.

notes: D edit: Captured as artefact but the telling part is spoken; a written reflection makes the artefact hold all the evidence.
P edit: 'reports the task as done alone' accuses of lying; the near-miss is doing it unaided only because the rule said so, with nothing learned said.

before.statement: Completes a task without AI that they could have done with it, and explains what doing it alone showed.
before.adult_sees: The educator sees the task done unaided and hears what it showed.
before.counter_example: Uses AI and reports the task as done alone.

behaviours.statement: Handles other people's data in a project according to a stated rule, such as consent and deletion, and shows the rule was followed.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the rule stated and evidence it was kept.
behaviours.counter_example: States a consent rule at the start and keeps the data after the project ends.

notes: P edit: 'Collects classmates' data without telling them' is a breach, not a look-alike; the near-miss is a rule stated and then not fully kept.

before.counter_example: Collects classmates' data without telling them.

could_not.detail: Below Grade 4 the school puts no screen in front of a child, so the Foundational behaviours are unplugged proxies: sequencing, giving instructions, real versus pretend, care of a shared device.

capabilities.name: Self & relationships
capabilities.observable_at_16: Shows resilience, emotional regulation, physical competence, empathy and responsible independence.

behaviours.statement: Names what they feel after a fall, a dispute or a lost game, in their own words, and chooses what to do next.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator hears a feeling named in the child's own words and sees the choice made; the note records the choice, never the words or the cause.
behaviours.counter_example: Is told by an adult what they are feeling and repeats it.

notes: R edit: Recording a small child's words in a hard moment files feelings, often with home causes, for ten years; note only the choice; a disclosure is safeguarding, not evidence.
D edit: 'A hard moment' is the observer's inference; name the visible trigger. Recording a distressed child's voice is heavier than a note, not lighter evidence.
E edit: In a hard moment I am with the child, not recording them; a dated note written afterwards is the only realistic capture.
P edit: My four-year-old's words about their feelings, recorded in their own voice and kept ten years, are not the school's to hold; note the choice, not the words.
chair edit: parent and rights converge: the note records the choice, never the words or the cause.

before.adult_sees: The educator hears the child's own words and sees the choice made.
before.statement: Says what they are feeling in a hard moment, in their own words, and chooses something to do about it.

behaviours.statement: Waits for a turn on the slide or with a toy without a reminder from an adult.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the wait with no adult prompt.
behaviours.counter_example: Waits only after an adult says their name.

behaviours.statement: Notices a classmate who is hurt or crying and does something for them, such as fetching an adult or sitting with them.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the noticing and the act that follows.
behaviours.counter_example: Joins the crowd around the hurt classmate to look, without doing anything for them.

notes: R edit: 'To get them in trouble' reads a motive into a small child and casts telling an adult as suspect, which safeguarding must never do; the look-alike is crowding to look.
D edit: Onlooking is what observers over-count as comforting; 'to get them in trouble' is a mind read and not a look-alike.
E edit: 'To get them in trouble' is a motive I cannot see; the look-alike I confuse is telling an adult and walking away.
P edit: 'to get them in trouble' reads a four-year-old's motive and accuses; the near-miss is noticing aloud and doing nothing for the classmate.
chair edit: rights seat's counter: telling an adult must never be cast as the lesser act (safeguarding); the look-alike is crowding to look.

before.counter_example: Reports the classmate to an adult to get them in trouble.

behaviours.statement: Manages their own bag, bottle and shoes at arrival and departure without an adult doing it for them, using any aids they have.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees the bag, bottle and shoes handled by the child, with their own aids if any, and no adult's hands on them.
behaviours.counter_example: Holds out a foot for an adult to put the shoe on.

notes: R edit: 'Without help' bars a child who uses an aid or adaptation from ever earning independence; independence means doing it with one's own aids and no adult doing it for them.
P edit: 'didi' assumes every home sends a helper and marks the children whose homes do; that word does not belong in a ten-year record.
chair edit: merged: the parent's concrete things with the rights seat's own aids.

before.statement: Manages their own bag, bottle and shoes at arrival and departure without help.
before.adult_sees: The educator sees the routine done without a didi.
before.counter_example: Waits for a didi to do it.

behaviours.statement: Runs, jumps with two feet together and balances on one foot for a count of three during play.
behaviours.adult_sees: The educator sees each movement done without a hand held.
behaviours.counter_example: Does the movement only with a hand held.
